To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the major surface glycoprotein of the protozoan parasite Leishmania donovanii, the lipophospholycan (LPG), inhibits the formation of multinucleated giant cells (syncytia) induced by human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV‐1) in vitro.
the lipophospholipid of Leishmania donavani is a potent inhibitor of HIV‐I‐mediated syncitium formation and virus infection.
LPG inhibits HIV‐1‐associated syncytium formation in a semiquantitative reporter assay and that it inhibits HIV‐ 1 infection and replication in an acute infection assay.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the inhibitory properties of LPG on HIV‐1‐related processes.
the inhibition by LPG of the early stages of HIV‐1 infection and replication, which is of particular relevance to understanding the pathogenic mechanisms underlying leishmaniasis and AIDS.
the identification of a natural molecule able to block HIV‐1 replication, a molecule that could be used in a prophylactic approach.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the LPG molecule from L. donovani is an inhibitor of HIV‐mediated syncytiogenesis and HIV‐1 replication, and that the inhibitory effect of LPG is probably due to its ability to modulate virus‐cell and/or cell‐cell fusion.

LPG acts as a strong inhibitor of early HIV‐1‐related events, such as attachment, entry, signal transduction and cell‐to-cell fusion, and that these effects are additive and lead to a significant reduction of HIV‐1 infectivity.

LPG is able to inhibit HIV‐1‐associated syncytium formation by acting at different levels in the virus life‐cycle, namely at the level of viral entry, at the level of signal transduction and at the level of virus‐mediating syncytium formation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

LPG, the major surface molecule from the Leishmania parasite, is able to inhibit HIV‐1‐associated events, such as syncytium formation or virus entry and that this inhibition is due to its effect on early events of the virus life cycle, such as virus binding and entry.

LPG, a major surface glycolipid of Leishmania donivani, is a strong inhibitor of the HIV‐1‐associated syncytium formation in a dose‐ and pretreatment‐dependent manner, which is likely to be mediated by a postbinding event.

the inhibition of HIV‐I‐mediated syncitium formation and virus production by LPG was due to a direct effect of LPG on the target cells, which was not mediated by a decrease of the expression of CD4 and other surface molecules.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LPG, the major surface molecule from the protozoan parasite Leishmania, is a potent inhibitor of HIV‐ 1 replication and that this inhibition is mediated at an early step in viral entry.
LPG is a potent inhibitor of both HIV‐1‐ mediated syncytium and virus replication.
LPG can inhibit HIV‐1‐associated syncytium formation as well as HIV‐1 replication at the entry stage.
